clue.text: Browne's hydriotaphia ..

parts.note: Sir Thomas Browne's 1658 treatise Hydriotaphia carries an English subtitle naming the interment of ashes in urns

explanation.surface: A reference to Sir Thomas Browne's meditation on ancient funeral urns, trailing off into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Browne's Hydriotaphia is subtitled Urn Burial; the dots lead into the next clue's opening dots.
explanation.definitionFit: The book's subtitle names it as a treatise on interment, the putting of the dead into the ground or an urn.

clue.text: Tweedsmuir article describes Annan Water novelist

an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Lord Tweedsmuir writes about a Scottish river.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Buchanan wrote the novel Annan Water (1883).
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Buchanan, Scottish poet and writer, published a novel of that name.

clue.text: Princess of Bolton

parts.note: Guy Bolton adapted the play about the woman claiming to be the Tsar's surviving daughter

explanation.surface: A royal lady from a Lancashire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bolton is a Lancashire town, but here it is Guy Bolton, who adapted the play Anastasia (1954).
explanation.definitionFit: The youngest daughter of Tsar Nicholas II was a Grand Duchess, the play's princess.

clue.text: … as a heretic, however, I am interred in black vulcanized rubber

indicators.note: being buried in something places the letter inside that word, so I goes into the rubber

parts.note: ebonite is hard black rubber hardened by vulcanizing

explanation.surface: Continuing Browne's theme of burial, a heretic imagines being buried in black rubber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'am interred in' puts I inside EBONITE. The Ebionites were an early Jewish-Christian sect deemed heretical.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebionites were an early sect whose views on Christ the Church condemned as unorthodox belief.

clue.text: Dickens's corrupt "gentleman" (Meldrum perhaps?) following posh car ()

indicators.note: following puts the jumbled name after the car

parts.note: Bentley is a luxury British car make

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the name in brackets may be a jumbled form

explanation.surface: A Dickensian cad, possibly named Meldrum, trails behind a luxury car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges MELDRUM to DRUMMLE. The empty brackets at the end are a print artefact.
explanation.definitionFit: The brutish suitor who marries Estella in Great Expectations is a rich but boorish so-called gentleman.

clue.text: Horne's hunter

parts.note: R. H. Horne wrote an epic poem about the giant huntsman of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A huntsman belonging to someone called Horne.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Hengist Horne published his epic poem Orion in 1843, famously priced at a farthing.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant hunter of Greek myth is the subject of Horne's epic.

explanation.walkthrough: Lewis is C. S. Lewis, not the Scottish island; Edmund Pevensie betrays the others but is crowned King.

clue.text: Wily Shakespearian character who smelled sweet savours and felt soft things

parts.note: the drunken tinker of the Shrew induction, whose surname means wily, wakes saying he smells sweet savours and feels soft things

explanation.walkthrough: In The Taming of the Shrew's induction the tinker says 'I smell sweet savours and I feel soft things'.
explanation.definitionFit: The tinker tricked into thinking himself a lord bears a surname meaning cunning.

clue.text: Premier Canadian author

definitions.meaning: Morley ... was a Toronto novelist and short-story writer

explanation.walkthrough: Two people share the surname: a British Prime Minister and a Canadian novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to a British Prime Minister and to the Toronto writer Morley.

clue.text: Its fortifications apparently not yet complete in Marlowe's day

definitions.text: Its fortifications apparently not yet complete in Marlowe's day

parts.words: Its fortifications apparently not yet complete in Marlowe's day
parts.note: Marlowe's Faustus speaks of 'the topless towers' of Troy, read jokingly as towers not yet given their tops

explanation.surface: A joke about building work left unfinished in Elizabethan times.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Faustus has 'Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships, / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?'; 'topless' is taken as unfinished.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Latin name for Troy, whose towers Marlowe famously called topless.

clue.text: Tati perhaps with French companion (Jonah's father)

explanation.surface: The French film director Jacques Tati is pictured with a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacques Tati was a French film-maker; his name here is just letters to rearrange, and 'with' joins the friend to them. Amittai is named in Jonah 1:1.
explanation.definitionFit: The Book of Jonah opens by naming the prophet as son of this man.

clue.text: Cathedral city Guide by Vidal?

definitions.meaning: an English county town with a famous Gothic cathedral
Gore Vidal wrote a 1984 historical novel about the President who guided the Union through the Civil War

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is Gore Vidal's novel named after the sixteenth US President, the nation's guide.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both an English cathedral city and the title of Gore Vidal's novel about a President.

clue.text: Giant in endless merchant ship

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter of the ship word is dropped

parts.note: an argosy is a large merchant vessel

explanation.surface: A giant is found aboard a big trading vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' takes the Y off ARGOSY. Argos (or Argus) was the hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the many-eyed watchman set over Io bore this name, a monstrous herdsman.

clue.text: Apt designation for Hero

explanation.walkthrough: Hero is a woman's name, so the feminine of hero is apt for her.

clue.text: A bit of a let-down for Lesbia, perhaps

a strong cold wind of southern France, here raised up in the surface

explanation.walkthrough: Frederic Mistral won the 1904 Nobel Prize; the mistral is a cold north wind down the Rhone valley.

clue.text: Occurrence illustrating attachment of first lady to old book

clue.text: It signifies no more than private opinion, said Hobbes

definitions.text: It signifies no more than private opinion, said Hobbes

parts.words: It signifies no more than private opinion, said Hobbes
parts.note: Leviathan says this word, of Greek origin, means merely a personal choice of opinion
